patient.chief_complaint: Three-day bilateral tingling, bilateral areflexia, and mild gait unsteadiness in a 22-year-old with no weakness — 2 weeks after Campylobacter gastroenteritis.
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. B. is a 22-year-old college student presenting to the ED with a 3-day history of bilateral tingling in her hands and feet. She had a clear Campylobacter gastroenteritis 2 weeks ago, confirmed by stool culture at a student health center. She recovered fully. Three days ago she developed bilateral hand and foot tingling. Yesterday she noticed her reflexes seemed absent when she tested them with her roommate (nursing student). She reports very mild gait unsteadiness but denies frank weakness — she walked to the ED. She has no facial symptoms, no diplopia, no dysphagia. She is very anxious. The ED physician considered a functional neurological disorder given the absence of objective weakness.

specialized_test.impression: This is an ABNORMAL nerve conduction study. 1. Mildly to moderately prolonged distal motor latencies and borderline-to-reduced conduction velocities in bilateral median and peroneal motor nerves; CMAP amplitudes preserved. 2. Absent sural sensory nerve action potentials bilaterally. 3. Absent F-waves bilaterally in median and peroneal nerves. 4. Absent H-reflex bilaterally. 5. EMG: no denervation activity. Pattern indicates a demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with proximal involvement and preserved motor axon integrity

cardiac_monitoring.impression: Continuous inpatient telemetry through the period of maximal weakness. Autonomic instability is present in about two thirds of patients with Guillain-Barré syndrome and is a leading cause of in-hospital death, so this recording is a monitoring requirement rather than a diagnostic test: it detects the bradyarrhythmias, pauses and blood-pressure lability that trigger ICU escalation, alongside serial respiratory function. Pauses beyond 3 seconds with blood-pressure lability constitute significant dysautonomia: continuous monitoring is maintained, atropine kept at the bedside, and suctioning treated as a provocative manoeuvre.

results.title: IVIG in Guillain-Barré syndrome: timing and efficacy
results.finding: Randomized controlled trials have demonstrated that IVIG initiated within two weeks of symptom onset shortens the time to recovery in GBS. The benefit of treatment beyond two weeks is less well established.

results.title: GBS natural history and respiratory involvement
results.finding: Population-based studies report that GBS typically progresses over 2–4 weeks. Approximately 20–30% of patients require mechanical ventilation at some point during the illness.

results.title: Brighton Collaboration diagnostic criteria for GBS
results.finding: The Brighton Collaboration case definition for GBS includes: bilateral flaccid limb weakness, decreased or absent deep tendon reflexes in weak limbs, symptom progression over up to 12 weeks, and absence of an identified alternative diagnosis. Electrodiagnostic studies contribute to case classification levels.

output.summary: IVIG and plasmapheresis have demonstrated efficacy in reducing time to recovery in GBS in randomized trials. Natural history data indicate potential for respiratory failure in a significant proportion of patients. Clinical correlation with individual patient findings is required.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Guillain-Barré syndrome, early AIDP (day 3, areflexia with early electrodiagnostic abnormalities)

differential.key_features: Cannot exclude at day 3 — reclassify if progression continues beyond 8 weeks.
Areflexia is not typical of myositis; CK elevation expected — different EMG pattern (myopathic units).
Possible mimic if outdoor exposure; thorough skin/scalp inspection for tick required; sensory symptoms are present here.
Abdominal pain or psychiatric symptoms typically precede; urine porphyrins are diagnostic; consider in atypical cases.
Episodic, fluctuating weakness with normal sensation and preserved reflexes; potassium normal here.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain CBC, CMP, HIV, anti-GM1/anti-GQ1b ganglioside antibodies, and stool culture / Campylobacter serology if recent diarrhea
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Mild leukocytosis / elevated inflammatory markers reflecting antecedent infection; ganglioside antibodies for variant typing; trigger identification (Campylobacter, CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, HIV)

optimal_actions.action: Order nerve conduction studies and needle EMG (EMG/NCS)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Demyelinating pattern (prolonged DML, conduction block, reduced CV, absent F-waves) consistent with AIDP, or reduced CMAP amplitudes in axonal variants (AMAN/AMSAN)

optimal_actions.action: Perform lumbar puncture for CSF analysis
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Albuminocytologic dissociation — elevated protein with cell count <10/μL; may be normal in the first week of illness

optimal_actions.action: Order bedside respiratory function testing (FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF) and repeat every 4–6 hours
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Baseline and serial FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF; deterioration to FVC <20 mL/kg, MIP worse than -30 cmH2O, or VC <40% predicted triggers ICU transfer / intubation

optimal_actions.action: Search the medical literature for IVIG vs plasma exchange evidence to guide disease-modifying therapy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: IVIG (0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days) and plasma exchange are equivalently effective first-line therapies; combination not superior

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions / contraindications for IVIG (renal function, IgA deficiency screen) and/or plasma exchange (coagulation, calcium, hemodynamics)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Confirmation that IVIG can be given safely (no severe renal impairment, no IgA deficiency) or that plasma exchange is appropriate (adequate vascular access, stable coagulation)

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a 12-lead ECG to screen for autonomic dysrhythmias and baseline QTc
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sinus tachycardia or bradycardia; conduction or repolarisation abnormalities reflecting autonomic involvement

optimal_actions.action: Start continuous inpatient cardiac telemetry for the period of maximal weakness and keep it running alongside serial respiratory function. Autonomic instability affects about two thirds of patients and is a leading cause of in-hospital death: bradyarrhythmias, pauses beyond 3 seconds and blood-pressure lability are what trigger ICU escalation
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Documentation of sinus pauses, bradyarrhythmias, BP lability, or non-sustained tachyarrhythmias

useless_tools.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: Document respiratory status (FVC/NIF) before committing to IVIG vs plasma exchange — severe respiratory compromise mandates ICU triage and may influence treatment choice and timing.
Renal function, IgA screen, and CBC must be reviewed before IVIG to mitigate renal failure, anaphylaxis (IgA-deficient patients), and aseptic meningitis risk.

critical_actions: Admit for serial respiratory and neurological monitoring given rapid early progression.
Initiate IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days even in early disease if Brighton level 1–2 clinical picture is met.
Repeat EMG/NCS at 7–14 days if initial study is normal or borderline — early studies may be falsely reassuring.
Repeat lumbar puncture in 7–10 days if initial CSF protein is normal — albuminocytologic dissociation often emerges at 1–2 weeks.
contraindicated_actions: Do not exclude GBS based on a normal early CSF or near-normal early EMG — both are well-described in days 1–7.
Do not delay IVIG/PLEX waiting for confirmatory tests if the clinical picture is convincing.
Do not give corticosteroids as monotherapy.
key_reasoning_points: GBS at day 3 may present with NORMAL CSF protein and NORMAL routine NCS — F-wave abnormalities and CSF protein elevation typically emerge later.
Areflexia + ascending progression in <4 weeks is sufficient clinical evidence to commence treatment under Brighton level 2–3.
Tick paralysis must be excluded by full skin / scalp examination in any case with rapid ascending paralysis.
Plan re-investigation at 7–14 days if early studies are equivocal — treatment should not wait.

red_herrings.data_point: Borderline / near-normal early CSF and EMG findings
red_herrings.intended_effect: Imply that GBS is excluded and lead to a delay in IVIG/PLEX initiation.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Early GBS commonly has minimal CSF and EMG abnormalities; clinical pattern + areflexia is sufficient to treat empirically.
